title: Slash commands
plain: A slash command is a message that starts with / and controls Claude Code itself, for example /help or /clear. Type / to see the list of commands you can use.
check: You send the message 'please run /clear now' as one line. What happens to the conversation, and what rule explains it?
rubric: Types / at the start of an empty message and the list of commands appears
Types a few letters after the / and the list gets shorter
Says that Claude Code runs a command only when it starts the message
try: In the terminal, type / on an empty prompt. A list of command names appears. Type three more letters, for example /sta, and watch the list get shorter. Press Backspace until the prompt is empty again. Desktop app: type / in the prompt box, or click the plus button and choose Slash commands.
pitfall: Wrong belief: every slash command is a fixed feature built into the program. Correct: skills appear in the list too, and a command works only at the start of your message.

title: Shell mode with !
plain: Shell mode runs a command you type yourself. Start a message with !. Claude Code runs the rest as a command and adds the output to the conversation.
check: You type '! git status' and press Enter. Where does the output appear, and who reads it besides you?
rubric: Types ! followed by git status (or ls) and sends it
Sees the command and its output in the conversation
Notices that Claude then comments on the output without being asked
try: In the terminal, type `! git status` at the empty prompt and press Enter. You see the command and its output, then a short comment from Claude. In a folder without git, the output is 'fatal: not a git repository'. If you typed ! by mistake, press Escape on the empty prompt to leave shell mode. Desktop app (local session): open the Terminal pane with Ctrl+` and run git status there.
pitfall: Wrong belief: shell mode is a safer way to run a command because Claude is not involved. Correct: the command runs with your rights and no permission prompt, and Claude reads the output.

title: Side questions with /btw
plain: A /btw side question asks about the session without adding the question or answer to the conversation. Claude answers only from what is already in the session and cannot open files or run commands.
check: A teammate asks what is in a file Claude has never opened. Why can /btw not answer that, and what would you use instead?
rubric: Says /btw sees the whole conversation so far, including what Claude already read
Says /btw has no tools, so it cannot read a new file or run a command
Chooses an ordinary message or a subagent for something new to find out
try: Type `/btw in one sentence, what have we done in this session so far?` and press Enter. A box with a short answer opens over the conversation. Press Escape to close it. Your main conversation does not contain the question or the answer. Type `/btw` alone to reopen the last answer. Desktop app: the same command opens a side chat.
pitfall: Wrong belief: /btw is a second chat that can look things up. Correct: it sees the whole conversation but has no tools, so it cannot find out anything new.

title: Skills
plain: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file of instructions for one kind of job. Claude loads it when the task fits its description, or you start it by typing /skill-name.
check: Why does a skill's short description matter more than its instructions when Claude decides whether to use the skill?
rubric: Finds a skill with /skills or the / menu and reads its description
Predicts one request that makes Claude load the skill by itself
Names the direct way to start it: / followed by the skill name
try: Type `/skills`. A list of skills appears: bundled ones, ones from ~/.claude/skills/ and ones from this project's .claude/skills/. Use the arrow keys to read two names and descriptions, then press Escape. Do not press Space or Enter on a skill: they change its visibility, and Escape saves that change. Desktop app: type / in the prompt box and read the entries.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a skill is a program that runs by itself. Correct: a skill is a text file of instructions, and by default only its short description is always visible to Claude.

title: Subagents
plain: A subagent is a helper that Claude starts for a side task. It works in its own separate context, with its own instructions and tools, and sends back only a short report.
check: Earlier you told Claude 'use tabs, not spaces'. Claude now hands a task to a subagent. What will the subagent know about that instruction, and how can you make sure it follows it?
rubric: Says a subagent starts with a fresh context and does not see the earlier conversation
Says a lasting rule belongs in CLAUDE.md (most subagents load it; the built-in Explore and Plan agents skip it), or must be repeated when Claude hands over the task
Names a job that suits a subagent, such as a search with long output, because only a short report comes back
try: Type: `Use a subagent to find every file in this project that contains the word TODO, and report only the file names.` A row appears with the subagent's name and a short task description. A list of file names comes back, possibly a moment later. Searching only reads files, so nothing should change. Type `/tasks` to see background work.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a subagent shares my chat memory. Correct: it starts fresh and sees only the task Claude writes for it, plus your CLAUDE.md files (the built-in Explore and Plan agents skip them); your output style does not shape its answers.

title: Hooks
plain: A hook is a command that Claude Code runs automatically at a fixed moment, such as before a tool runs. Hooks are usually set in settings files, and Claude cannot skip them.
check: A PreToolUse hook finds a forbidden command and ends with exit code 1. What happens to the command, and what one change makes the hook do its job?
rubric: Names events such as PreToolUse (before a tool runs), PostToolUse (after it) and Stop (when Claude finishes)
Says exit code 2 blocks the action on events that can block, and the script's stderr text goes to Claude
Says exit code 1 is only a non-blocking error on most events, so the action goes on
try: Type `/hooks`. A read-only list opens with the hooks from your settings files and plugins, and where each one comes from. Select one to read the command it runs, then press Escape. You may see none yet. Choose All events at the end of the list to read the names of the moments a hook can use. Desktop app: ask Claude `Which hooks are set in my settings files? List the event names only.`
pitfall: Wrong belief: a rule in CLAUDE.md is as strong as a hook. Correct: CLAUDE.md is advice Claude usually follows, but Claude Code itself runs a hook, with your full user rights.

title: MCP servers
plain: An MCP server gives Claude Code extra tools, such as access to an issue tracker or a database. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that defines how it connects.
check: A tutorial says to run `claude mcp add --transport http helper https://helper.example.net/mcp`. What would you find out before you press Enter, and why?
rubric: Finds out who runs the server and whether that source can be trusted
Says what the server could read or change once connected, such as your data or accounts
Names the risk that a server which fetches outside content can carry hidden instructions (prompt injection)
try: Type `/mcp`. A list of your MCP servers opens, each with a status such as connected or needs authentication. The list is empty if you have none. Change nothing and close the list. In a normal terminal, `claude mcp list` prints the servers with a status next to each. Desktop app: click the plus button and open Connectors.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a server from a directory or tutorial has been checked, so it is safe. Correct: Anthropic reviews directory listings against criteria but does not security-audit or manage any MCP server, and a connected server can read your data and give Claude hidden instructions in its text (prompt injection).

title: Output styles
plain: An output style is a set of instructions that changes how Claude answers: its role, tone, length and format. Built-in styles are Proactive, Concise, Explanatory and Learning; you switch with /output-style.
check: You want a formatter to run after every file edit, without exception. Why is an output style the wrong tool for that, and what is the right one?
rubric: Says an output style is an instruction that Claude follows, so it cannot guarantee that something happens every time
Names a hook as the right tool for a step that must run after every file edit
Runs /output-style, reads which style is marked as the current one, and switches to Concise or Explanatory to see the next answer change
try: In the terminal, type `/output-style` with nothing after it. The styles are listed and the current one is marked. Write its name down. Then type `/output-style concise` and ask `What does git status show?` Notice the shorter answer. Switch back with `/output-style` and the name you wrote down. The command saves your choice in .claude/settings.local.json. Desktop app: set the outputStyle field in a settings file, for example .claude/settings.local.json.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a style makes Claude more capable or makes it behave the same way every time. Correct: a style is an instruction about tone and format, so it does not guarantee behavior, and subagents ignore it.

title: Settings files and scopes
plain: Claude Code reads settings from JSON files at four levels: user (all your projects), shared project, local project (only you), and managed (set by an organization).
check: Your team's .claude/settings.json sets model to sonnet and your ~/.claude/settings.json sets it to opus. Which model starts in that project, and in which file would you put an override that affects only you?
rubric: Orders the levels: managed first, then command line, then project local, then shared project, then user
Says .claude/settings.json is shared once committed to git, while .claude/settings.local.json stays on this computer (add it to .gitignore if you create it by hand)
Puts a personal exception for one project in .claude/settings.local.json
try: In the terminal, type `/status` and find the line Setting sources. It names each settings file Claude Code loaded, such as User settings. Then type `! ls .claude` and look for settings.json and settings.local.json. If /status does not open in the Desktop app, run `ls .claude` in the Terminal pane.
pitfall: Wrong belief: my user settings always win, and files in .claude stay on my computer. Correct: project settings outrank user settings, managed settings outrank all, and .claude/settings.json is shared through git.

title: Models and effort
plain: A model is the version of Claude that does the work. Aliases such as sonnet, opus and haiku point to a current model of that kind. Effort sets how much it reasons before answering.
check: You must rename one variable in a small file, and later track down a bug that only happens sometimes. How would you set the effort for each job, and what do you give up when you raise it?
rubric: Names the trade: a stronger model or higher effort gives deeper work but uses your allowance faster, and max can overthink
Picks lower effort or a smaller model for a small, clear change such as a rename
Picks higher effort for risky work, such as a bug with edge cases
try: In the terminal, type `/effort status`. It prints your current effort level. Then type `/status` and read the model name. Change nothing. Desktop app: use the dropdown next to the send button for the model. Press Ctrl+Shift+E (Cmd+Shift+E on macOS) for the effort menu.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the biggest model on the highest effort is always best. Correct: it is slower and uses more allowance, so raise effort only when the result is not good enough.

title: Usage limits and cost
plain: Subscription plans give a usage allowance, counted in a session window of about five hours and a weekly window. /usage shows what you used and when each window resets.
check: You ask one short question in a conversation that has been open all day and your usage jumps. What explains it, and what do you do before the next unrelated task?
rubric: Runs /usage and finds the plan usage bars or the cost of this session
Says which window resets first, the session window or the weekly one
Names two habits that make usage last longer, such as /clear between tasks and a smaller model
try: Type `/usage`. On a subscription plan you see usage bars for your plan limits and when each resets. With an API key you see the cost of this session. Read it, then close it. Desktop app: click the usage ring next to the model picker.
pitfall: Wrong belief: every message costs the same, so only the number of messages matters. Correct: Claude Code sends the whole conversation each time, so a long conversation costs more per message.

title: Writing a good request
plain: A good request says where to work, what is wrong or wanted, and how you will check it is done. It also keeps to one task. Specific requests need fewer corrections than vague ones.
check: How would you rewrite 'make the page look better' so Claude knows which page, what 'better' means, and how to check it?
rubric: Names the place: a file, a page or a feature
Describes the symptom or the wanted result in words, not only 'better'
Says how you will both know it worked, such as a test to run or text to see
try: Pick one small change in your project. Send a request in three parts, for example: `In README.md, add one sentence under the first heading that says what this project is for. Then show me the new line so I can check it.` Use another text file if you have no README.md. Claude edits one file and shows the line. To undo it, type `Undo that`.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Claude knows what I mean without details, so a short vague request is faster. Correct: naming the file, the symptom and the check usually saves rounds of correction; vague questions are fine only when you explore.

title: Checking Claude's work
plain: Verification means proving that Claude's change works instead of trusting the word 'done'. Ask Claude to run the tests or commands that check it, and read the diff (the list of changed lines) yourself.
check: Claude reports 'Done, the login bug is fixed.' Which two things do you do before you believe it, and what does each prove?
rubric: Finds or asks for the command that checks the project (tests, a build or a script) and runs it
Reads the printed result, not only Claude's summary, and knows tests prove only what they test
Opens the diff and matches every changed file to what was asked
try: After Claude has changed a file in a git project, type `/diff`. A list of changed files opens, each with its added and removed line counts. Select a file with the arrow keys and press Enter to read its lines. Escape goes back, and Escape on the list closes it. In fullscreen mode, /diff opens a panel beside the chat instead; run /diff again to close it. Then ask `Run the tests and show me the output.` Desktop app: open the diff pane with Ctrl+Shift+D (Cmd+Shift+D on macOS).
pitfall: Wrong belief: if Claude says the work is done, it is correct. Correct: Claude stops when the work looks done, so only a check you can see, such as test output, shows that it works.
